relevant_findings: Ceiling finish quality is highly sensitive to lighting angle, sheen, and surface uniformity.
Flat sheens conceal defects better than matte; matte finishes require higher inspection discipline.
Spray + backroll improves uniformity on ceilings but increases labor and protection requirements.
condition_drivers: Ceiling geometry (vaulted/tray increases reach and inspection difficulty).
Lighting angle and natural light exposure.
Finish sheen selection (matte increases defect visibility).
quality_differences: QL-3: Functional finish with limited sanding between coats.
QL-4: Increased sanding and inspection, especially for visible transitions.
QL-5: Strict inspection discipline and conservative application for high-visibility ceilings.
failure_modes: Roller lines or lap marks due to uneven application.
Shadowing and telegraphing under raking light.
notes_for_materials_manager: Ceiling finishes typically favor flat/matte paints with good hide and minimal flashing.
Consumables include rollers, extension poles, masking, and spray filters/tips.
notes_for_sop_librarian: Include sanding between coats as quality-driven repeated tasks.
Inspection rounds should increase with sheen visibility and ceiling geometry.
notes_for_estimation_engineer: Use SF measurement; vaulted ceilings should include geometry factor.
Application method significantly affects production rate.
uncertainties: Final lighting conditions may differ from inspection lighting.
Matte vs flat sheen performance varies by manufacturer.
